story: The building at 22 South Williams Street was built in 1886. The Wright brothers rented it from 1895 to 1897. The bicycle store was on the main floor, and their printing shop was on the second floor.
In 1896, while they were here, the brothers started selling bicycles of their own design, the Van Cleve and the St. Clair.

This is the only one of the Wrights' six shops still standing, and the only one still on its original foundation. The Wright Flyer was not built here. It was built at their last shop, on West Third Street. This building became a National Historic Landmark in 1990.
stops.fact: It is the only one of the Wrights' six shops still standing on its original spot.
stops.disputed: Many people think the Wrights built their first airplane in this shop. Wikipedia says the Wright Flyer was built at their last shop, at 1127 West Third Street.

story: Dayton banker Torrence Huffman owned this field and let the Wright brothers use it starting in 1904. They tested the Wright Flyer II here from April 1904, and made about 150 flights in 1904 and 1905.

One timed flight is on record. On November 16, 1904, Orville flew about 1,760 feet in just over 40 seconds. The 1905 Wright Flyer III came out of this work. The Wrights thought of it as the first practical airplane.

In 1910 the Wright Company moved here and ran the Wright Flying School, which trained more than 100 pilots, including Hap Arnold. The Army bought the field in 1917. In 1948 the area joined Patterson Field to form Wright-Patterson Air Force Base. Huffman Prairie became a National Historic Landmark in 1990.
stops.fact: The Wrights flew about 150 times here in 1904 and 1905.
stops.disputed: Many people think the Wrights learned to fly only at Kitty Hawk. Wikipedia says the Flyer III, which they considered the first practical airplane, grew out of testing here.

The Wrights first flew at Huffman Prairie in 1903.
claims.why: Their work at Huffman Prairie began in 1904.

story: The Flyer III was built in the winter of 1904 and 1905 and first flew on June 23, 1905. After a crash in July, the Wrights rebuilt it with bigger tail surfaces and a separate control for the rudder.
On October 5, 1905, Wilbur circled over Huffman Prairie for 24.2 miles. The flight lasted 39 minutes and 23 seconds. The Wrights thought of the Flyer III as their first practical airplane.

Its parts were held in Massachusetts from 1911 until Orville asked for them back in 1946. It was restored between 1947 and 1950, and craftsmen estimated that 60 to 85 percent of the original material survived. The wingspan is 40 feet 4 inches.
stops.fact: Wikipedia says it is the only fixed-wing aircraft designated a National Historic Landmark.
stops.disputed: Many people think the Wrights' first airplane in 1903 was their best. Wikipedia says the 1905 Flyer III was the first practical and dependable one.

claims.t: Wilbur flew the Flyer III about 24 miles on October 5, 1905.
The Flyer III is on display at the Smithsonian in Washington, D.C.

stops.clue: Go to the Paul Laurence Dunbar House in Dayton. Look for a red-brick house with a decorated front porch and a sign for the state memorial.

story: The house at 219 Paul Laurence Dunbar Street, then called North Summit Street, was built in 1894. Dunbar bought it for his mother, Matilda, in June 1904. He lived here until he died in the house in 1906.
Matilda lived here until her death on February 24, 1934. She kept his books, manuscripts and study just as he left them.
Ohio bought the house in 1936 and dedicated it as the first state memorial to an African American. It became a National Historic Landmark on December 29, 1962.
stops.fact: His mother kept his study exactly as he left it.
stops.disputed: Many people think a famous poet must have lived in a grand mansion. Wikipedia describes a modest brick house built in 1894 that Dunbar bought for his mother.
